LECTURER: Today I want to look at coral reefs, and in particular at the phenomenon known as coral bleaching, which has become one of the most visible signs of a warming ocean.
First, a reminder of what coral actually is. A coral reef is built by tiny animals called polyps, each only a few millimetres across. Polyps are related to jellyfish, and they live in huge colonies, producing a hard skeleton of calcium carbonate beneath them. Over thousands of years these skeletons accumulate to form a reef.
What's less obvious is that most reef-building corals depend on a partnership. Inside the tissue of the polyps live microscopic algae. These algae carry out photosynthesis, and they pass most of the sugars they produce to the coral. In some species, this supplies up to ninety per cent of the coral's energy. In return, the algae receive shelter and the nutrients they need. The algae also give coral much of its colour.
So what happens during bleaching? When the water becomes too warm, even by just one or two degrees above the normal summer maximum for several weeks, this relationship breaks down. The algae start to produce harmful chemicals, and the coral responds by expelling them. Without the algae, the coral's tissue becomes transparent, and we see the white skeleton underneath. That's why it's called bleaching.
It's important to understand that a bleached coral is not necessarily dead. If temperatures return to normal fairly quickly, the coral can take in new algae and recover. However, if the stress continues, the coral starves, and it becomes vulnerable to disease. Recovery of a whole reef can take a decade or more.
Temperature isn't the only cause. Bleaching can also be triggered by pollution, by unusually low tides that expose corals to the air, and by run-off from farms carrying sediment and fertiliser. But the large-scale events we've seen recently, affecting reefs across entire oceans, are linked to marine heatwaves.
Researchers are now exploring ways to help. One approach involves breeding corals that are more tolerant of heat and transplanting them onto damaged reefs. Another focuses on reducing local pressures, such as overfishing, so that reefs are in a stronger condition when heat stress occurs. But most scientists agree these are only partial solutions. In the long term, the survival of reefs depends on limiting the rise in sea temperatures.

LECTURER: In this session we're looking at one of the most remarkable examples of communication in the animal kingdom: the dance language of the honeybee.
The story begins with the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who studied bees for decades in the early twentieth century and was later awarded a Nobel Prize for his work. Von Frisch noticed that when a forager bee found a good source of food, other bees from the same hive soon arrived at that source, even though the first bee hadn't led them there. Somehow, information about the location was being shared inside the hive.
Through careful observation, often using glass-walled hives, he identified two main types of dance. The first is the round dance. The bee simply runs in small circles on the comb. This tells the others that food is close to the hive, typically within about fifty metres, but it doesn't give a precise direction. The other bees pick up the scent of the flowers from the dancer's body and search the area nearby.
The second type, the waggle dance, is far more informative. Here the bee runs in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side, then loops back and repeats the run. Two key pieces of information are encoded. The first is direction. Inside the dark hive, the bee dances on a vertical surface, and the angle of the straight run relative to vertical represents the angle between the food source and the sun. So if the bee waggles straight up, the food is in the direction of the sun.
The second is distance. The duration of the waggle run indicates how far away the food is: the longer the waggle, the further the flight. Interestingly, bees seem to measure distance not in metres but by the visual flow of the landscape passing beneath them during flight.
Von Frisch's conclusions were challenged for many years. Some researchers argued that bees found food mainly by smell. It was only later, with experiments using robotic bees and radar tracking of individual foragers, that the dance hypothesis was strongly confirmed.
Finally, it's worth noting that the dance isn't fixed. Bees adjust their dances as the sun moves across the sky during the day, which implies they compensate for time. And the enthusiasm of the dance, meaning the number of repeats, reflects the quality of the food source.

• Waggle dance: angle of run shows direction relative to the (3) ______
• Length of waggle run indicates (4) ______
• Dance theory later confirmed using robotic bees and (5) ______ tracking

LECTURER: Good morning. Today's lecture is about a technology we take so much for granted that we rarely think about it: paper.
Before paper, people wrote on many different materials. In ancient Egypt, they used papyrus, made from strips of a reed that grew along the Nile. In Europe, the usual material for important documents was parchment, made from animal skin. Parchment was durable, but it was also very expensive. A single large book might require the skins of a hundred or more animals.
Paper as we understand it was developed in China. Traditional accounts credit an official called Cai Lun, who in the year 105 presented a method to the emperor. However, archaeologists have since found fragments of paper that are older than this, so it's more accurate to say that Cai Lun improved and standardised an existing process. Early Chinese paper was made from plant fibres, such as the bark of the mulberry tree, along with old rags and fishing nets. These materials were soaked, beaten into a pulp, spread on a screen and left to dry.
For several centuries the technique remained largely within East Asia. It reached the Islamic world in the eighth century, and the city of Samarkand, in Central Asia, became an important centre of production. From there, paper-making spread to Baghdad, Damascus and Cairo, and eventually across North Africa into Spain. By the thirteenth century, paper mills were operating in Italy, where craftsmen introduced important innovations, including the use of water power to beat the pulp, and watermarks to identify the maker.
In Europe, the main raw material for paper remained linen rags for hundreds of years. This created a problem. As demand for paper grew, especially after the invention of the printing press in the fifteenth century, there simply weren't enough rags. There are records of rag shortages and even laws restricting their export.
The solution came in the nineteenth century, when methods were developed to make paper from wood pulp. This made paper dramatically cheaper and allowed the expansion of newspapers and mass education. But it had a disadvantage: wood-pulp paper often contained acids which caused it to turn yellow and become brittle over time. This is why many books from the late nineteenth century are now in worse condition than much older ones made from rag paper.

• European paper made from (4) ______ rags → shortages after printing press
• 19th-century wood-pulp paper: contained (5) ______, so became yellow and brittle

LECTURER: This afternoon we're turning to urban climates, and specifically to the urban heat island effect. Put simply, this is the tendency for cities to be warmer than the surrounding countryside. The difference is often modest during the day, but at night it can be dramatic, sometimes as much as ten degrees in large cities on calm, clear nights.
Why does this happen? There are several contributing factors. The first concerns surfaces. Materials such as asphalt and concrete absorb a great deal of solar radiation during the day and release it slowly as heat after sunset. Dark surfaces are particularly effective at this because they have a low albedo, which means they reflect only a small proportion of the sunlight that falls on them.
The second factor is the shortage of vegetation. In rural areas, plants release water vapour through their leaves, a process called transpiration, and this has a cooling effect, rather like sweating does for the human body. In cities, where much of the ground is sealed, this cooling is greatly reduced.
Third, the geometry of the city matters. Tall buildings close together create what are known as urban canyons. Heat that is radiated from the streets is trapped between buildings rather than escaping to the sky. Tall buildings can also block the wind, which would otherwise carry heat away.
Finally, there is heat produced directly by human activity: vehicles, factories and, increasingly, air-conditioning units, which ironically pump heat out into the streets in order to cool the interiors.
The consequences are significant. Higher night-time temperatures prevent people's bodies from recovering after hot days, and during heatwaves this contributes to increased mortality, particularly among elderly people. Higher temperatures also increase energy consumption and can worsen air quality.
So what can be done? Cities around the world are experimenting with several strategies. One is planting trees along streets, which provide shade and also cool the air through transpiration. Another is the installation of green roofs, covered with plants. A third approach is using cool materials, for example painting roofs white or using lighter-coloured paving, which raises the albedo. Some cities have also restored rivers that had been covered over, as open water helps cool the surrounding area. None of these measures is sufficient on its own, but studies suggest that combined, they can reduce local temperatures by several degrees.

LECTURER: Today I'd like to examine the relationship between sleep and memory, an area where research has advanced rapidly over the last twenty years.
Let's begin with a basic distinction. When we learn something new, the memory is initially fragile. To become stable and long-lasting, it must undergo a process called consolidation. For a long time, it was assumed that consolidation simply happened gradually over time. What researchers now know is that much of it takes place while we sleep.
Sleep isn't a single uniform state. Over the course of a night, we cycle through different stages roughly every ninety minutes. Two stages are especially important for memory. The first is slow-wave sleep, or deep sleep, which is concentrated in the first half of the night. The second is REM sleep, named after the rapid eye movements that accompany it. This is when most vivid dreaming occurs, and it's more common towards the morning.
During slow-wave sleep, a region of the brain called the hippocampus, which acts as a kind of temporary store for new information, appears to replay the day's experiences. Recordings in rats have shown that patterns of neural activity seen while the animal explored a maze are repeated, in compressed form, during subsequent sleep. This replay is thought to help transfer memories to the cortex for long-term storage.
REM sleep, on the other hand, seems to be particularly involved in emotional memories and in the integration of new information with existing knowledge. Some studies suggest that people are better at finding creative solutions to problems after a period of REM sleep, perhaps because the brain makes unexpected connections.
What happens when we don't sleep? In a typical experiment, participants learn a list of word pairs in the evening. Half sleep normally; the other half are kept awake. The next day, those who slept recall significantly more. Interestingly, even a short daytime nap of around an hour can produce measurable benefits.
There are practical implications here, especially for students. Staying up all night before an exam may feel productive, but it's likely to undermine the very consolidation that makes revision effective. Similarly, there is growing concern about adolescents, whose natural sleep patterns shift later, but who must wake early for school. Several studies have found that starting school later in the morning is associated with improved attendance and grades.

LECTURER: Today's topic is the placebo effect, which has fascinated doctors and researchers for centuries and remains surprisingly controversial.
A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill or an injection of salt water. The placebo effect refers to a genuine improvement in a patient's condition that results not from the treatment itself, but from the patient's belief or expectation that it will help.
The effect is most clearly seen in conditions that involve subjective experience, particularly pain, but also nausea, fatigue and depression. In some pain studies, a substantial proportion of patients given a placebo report significant relief. And this isn't just imagination. Brain-imaging studies have shown that placebos can trigger the release of the body's own natural painkillers, known as endorphins.
Several factors influence the strength of the effect. Interestingly, the appearance of the treatment matters. Two placebo pills tend to work better than one. Injections often produce a stronger effect than pills. And even the colour of tablets can make a difference. The attitude of the doctor is also important. Patients who are treated warmly and with confidence tend to respond better.
Perhaps most surprising is the finding that placebos can work even when patients know they're taking one. In so-called open-label trials, patients with certain conditions were told honestly that they were receiving a placebo, yet many still reported improvement. The reasons for this are still debated.
There's also a darker side, known as the nocebo effect. In other words, negative expectations can themselves cause symptoms. If patients expect side effects, they're more likely to experience them. In some trials, people taking a placebo have reported headaches or dizziness simply because those symptoms were listed as possible side effects.
Why does all this matter for medicine? Above all, because it affects how we test new drugs. If we simply gave a drug to patients and measured whether they improved, we couldn't tell whether the drug or the expectation was responsible. That's why the standard method is the randomised controlled trial, where one group receives the drug and another receives a placebo. Ideally, the trial is double-blind, meaning that neither the patients nor the researchers know who is receiving which. A new drug is only considered effective if it performs significantly better than the placebo.

• Nocebo effect: negative (4) ______ can produce side effects
• Drug testing: randomised, ideally (5) ______ trials

LECTURER: This morning we're looking at a question that has puzzled engineers for a long time: why have so many Roman concrete structures lasted for two thousand years, when much modern concrete begins to crack and crumble within decades?
Let's start with the ingredients. Modern concrete is typically made from Portland cement, water, sand and gravel. Roman concrete was different. Its binder was a mixture of lime and volcanic ash. The best ash came from the area around the Bay of Naples, near a town called Pozzuoli, which is why this material is known today as pozzolana.
When lime, volcanic ash and water are mixed, a chemical reaction produces a strong, stable binding material. The Romans didn't understand the chemistry, of course, but through long experience they knew which ingredients worked best, and the engineer and writer Vitruvius described their methods in detail.
Some of the most impressive examples are harbour structures, such as piers and breakwaters, built in seawater. For modern concrete, seawater is a serious problem, as it causes the steel reinforcement inside to corrode. But Roman marine concrete appears to have become stronger over time.
